title: Another Raytracer
desc: A WebGPU path tracer with fog, rainbow glass, teapots, fractals, and depth of field.
text: A progressive path tracer in a WebGPU compute shader: balls, flat panels, Utah teapots, brilliant cut diamonds, Menger sponges and Mandelbulbs, in paint, varnished paint, metal, glass and light. Drag to orbit, shift-drag or right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom; on a phone, pinch to zoom and drag two fingers to pan. Click or tap anything to select it and focus on it. Each scene opens with a line saying what it is, with arrows to the next; ← and → do the same. The URL keeps the scene, the view, any edits and any changed settings, so the address bar is a shareable link. Keys: space pauses, r resets the view, d toggles the denoiser, t cycles tone curves, h toggles HDR, n shows refining tiles, Esc deselects. Scenes: cornell : a Cornell-box hallway lit by a ceiling panel, with mirror, glass, amber glass, gold and glossy balls veach : the multiple importance sampling test scene from Eric Veach's thesis shafts (the default): a foggy room lit through window blinds caustics : glass balls focusing light into their shadows teapots : a glass teapot the color of tea, glazed china and gold, lit like a product photo: a softbox, a dim fill, and strip lights behind that outline the glass fractals : a glass Menger sponge casting a lattice of caustics, a gold Mandelbulb, and a white sponge lit down its tunnels lasers : a ball lens: seven parallel green laser beams through a slightly cloudy glass ball in a hazy room, crossing behind it, the outer ones closer (spherical aberration). Each beam lies on the path Snell's law gives, which was worked out separately and projected onto a render to check: beams 8.5 off the axis cross 11.5 past the ball's center, 3 off cross 14.6 diamond : a big round brilliant in a jeweler's light tent: a ring of softboxes that light whole facets, 40 small lights for sparkle and fire, and one small bright light behind it whose light the stone scatters into its shadow. Little gets through: a brilliant sends most light back out the top mirrors : two facing mirrors reflecting glowing orbs into the distance bokeh : balls on a walnut table, with fairy lights blurred into discs sunset : a low sun, a physically based sky, and hazy air glowing around the sun neon : a dark gallery lit by colored tubes, after Dan Flavin rgb : red, green and blue lights casting cyan, magenta and yellow shadows window : a dusty attic lit only by late sun through a round stained glass window set deep in the wall, ruby, amber, green and cobalt in four quarters, which casts four colored beams through the haze onto the floorboards, rippled by the old wavy glass, in a whitewashed room lit only by that light and what it bounces Editing : the Objects folder changes whatever is selected (outlined in gold): its material, color, gloss, roughness, brightness, size, a teapot's, diamond's or fractal's turn, a sponge's levels of holes or a Mandelbulb's power, and glass's frost, index of refraction and haze. Drag a selected ball or teapot to move it. add a ball , add a teapot and add a fractal drop one on the floor in view, clear of what's there; Backspace deletes; undo all edits restores the scene. Walls and floors can be lights too: make Cornell's ceiling one for the classic soft-shadowed box. How it renders: Light : each bounce aims a shadow ray at one light, picked by how bright it looks from there, within the cone a ball covers or the solid angle a panel covers (Ureña's spherical rectangles), and also bounces at random. Multiple importance sampling weighs the two. Paths end at random once they carry little light. Materials : rough reflections are GGX microfacets, sampled by visible normals, with the light lost between facets added back (Turquin). Reflections follow Fresnel: varnish reflects 4% head on and nearly all at grazing angles, metal whitens toward grazing, and glass uses the exact formula. Colored glass absorbs with distance. title: Island
desc: Millions of years in seconds: an island rises, rivers carve its valleys, and rainforest, desert and ice spread with the climate.
text: The crust under the island rises, rivers cut down into it, and soil creeps downhill, following the standard landscape evolution equation dh/dt = U − K Q^m · S + D ∇²h where U is uplift, Q is the river's discharge (all the rain falling upstream of a point), S is the slope to the next point downstream and D is how fast soil creeps. River cutting is solved implicitly down the drainage tree (Braun & Willett 2013, the method behind FastScape), so it is stable with 2,000-year steps. Hollows fill into lakes that spill over their lowest rim (priority flood, Barnes 2014), and rivers end at the sea, which they can't cut below. What the rivers cut away travels downstream and settles in still water: lakes fill in from where rivers enter, and at the coast it spreads down a gentle slope from each river mouth into a shelf. Rain comes in on the wind. Air climbing the island's broad slopes drops more rain, and it dries out as it crosses, so the windward side is wet and the lee is dry. It cools 6.5 °C per kilometer of height. Plants and soil send part of the rain back to the air, following Budyko's curve, so only the rest reaches rivers: in hot, dry places that's almost none on average, though bare ground still sheds up to 30% of its rain in storms. Plant cover follows how the rain compares with what warm air could take up, and roots hold soil, so bare ground erodes about 7 times faster than forest. Biomes come from the same two numbers (Whittaker's biomes, with UNEP's aridity bands): rainforest, forest, conifer forest, savanna, grassland, dry scrub, desert, tundra, and ice and snow. The Rain setting is the average over the land; tap a spot to see what grows there and how much rain falls. Turn down the rain to watch the lee become desert badlands, or the temperature to bring tundra down to the coast and snow onto the peaks. node island/test.js checks that at steady state every river's slope matches the exact answer U / (K Q^m), that sediment is conserved to a part in 10¹³, that the windward side is wetter, that Budyko's evaporation hits its known points, and that erosion peaks in semi-arid climates, as Langbein and Schumm found in real river basins (near 300 mm of rain a year), because there's runoff to move soil but too little for plants to hold it. Tap or click the land to follow a raindrop to the sea and see how much water flows past. Pick Raise or Lower to sculpt (drag to paint; on a phone, two fingers still zoom and pan), and watch the rivers find new routes. Lower the sea to expose the shelf, or raise it to drown the valleys. The camera drifts around the island until you take it. Space pauses. The URL keeps the island's seed and any changed settings. Rivers are drawn several times wider than real rivers (12 m + 70 m × √(flow in m³/s)) so creeks still show from across the island. Simplifications: sediment only settles in lakes and the sea, so rivers never build floodplains or fans on land; the rock is the same everywhere; there are no waves eating at the coast; and plants are always in balance with the climate, since they settle in far less than one 2,000-year step. The rain model is a simple sweep along the wind, not a weather simulation, and evaporation is a rough fit to temperature.

title: Lambdagator
desc: Watch lambda calculus run, drawn as hungry alligators eating each other.
text: It's organized as 23 short lessons in four chapters, shown as a path across the top, each with a sentence on what to notice. Finished lessons get checked off, and when one ends, Next goes on to the next. To try your own expression, open "Write your own" ( \ or λ for lambda, single-letter variables, λab.x is short for λa.λb.x ). It's drawn as Bret Victor's Alligator Eggs: each lambda is a hungry alligator guarding its family, each variable is an egg the color of the alligator it belongs to, and old gray alligators group things like parentheses. An alligator eats whatever is to its right, then dies, and each of its eggs hatches into a copy of what it ate. Nothing moves until you press Next. Before each step, the hungry alligator opens its mouth and the caption says what will happen; Next plays it: the meal shrinks into the mouth, then flies out to each of its eggs, growing back to full size as the eggs crack open and the alligator dies. "⏩ Fast forward" plays the rest quickly (or all of it again, if it's finished), speeding up through the middle of long runs and slowing down at the end. Underneath, the expression is written in the usual notation, colored to match the alligators, with the part about to change underlined. Reduction is normal order (leftmost, outermost first), so it finds a normal form whenever one exists. Between steps, click any hungry alligator with something to its right to have it eat next instead. Variables get renamed to avoid capture, but that isn't animated, since the colors already tell the alligators apart. Uppercase names like TRUE , ADD , and Y are built in, numbers are Church numerals, and you can define your own on separate lines ( TWICE = λfx.f(fx) ). Nothing is hidden behind the names: under each lesson's goal is every definition it depends on, built up from plain lambdas (factorial lists Y, TRUE, FALSE, ISZERO, MUL, PRED, the numbers, and FACT itself). Names show up as chips with a faint drawing of their alligators inside, and unfold only when they're applied, with a caption explaining what they mean. When part of the expression turns back into exactly something with a name, like the recursion in the factorial example becoming FACT again, it's folded back into a chip so big expressions stay readable. The final result is recognized if it matches a name or number. To see why names like TRUE = λab.a and MUL = λmnf.m(nf) are defined the way they are, each one has a "Why?" that works backward from what it needs to do to the lambda that does it, with a "Try it" button. The "What the names do" examples show each one in action on eggs with no alligator, which stand in for anything, like x and y in algebra: 3 f x hatches into f(f(f x)) . The "What is this?" dialog explains what lambda calculus is and why it matters, illustrates the rules, and says how the alligators map to the usual notation. Files: lambda.js : parsing, reduction steps, and writing terms out gatorLayout.js : where each alligator and egg goes stage.js : draws layouts and animates between them animate.js : the animation for each kind of step captions.js : what the captions say names.js : what each built-in name means and why it's built that way examples.js : the lessons help.js : the "What is this?" and "Why?" dialogs, and the list of built-in names main.js : the controls and stepping through test/lambda.test.js : tests for lambda.js . Run them with node test lambdagator/test/ .test.js The older text-based interpreter is in ../lambdaCalculus .

title: Language Model Visualizer
desc: Watch the inner workings of a tiny GPT doing inference
text: langViz A tiny GPT (4 layers, d_model 96, 4 heads, 8.1k-token vocab, 1.2M params) trained on the KJV bible, running inference entirely in the browser in vanilla JS. The page is a near-chrome-free ambient piece: it auto-generates KJV-flavored text one token at a time from a fixed prompt (looping every 96 generated tokens) and renders a pannable/zoomable visualization of the whole network lighting up as it infers. On-screen controls are a prompt box and transport at the top and a stage rail along the bottom; the sampling constants are fixed in js/main.js . The tokenizer is word-level with a character fallback : the 8k most common words/punctuation are whole tokens (99.3% of the corpus), and any rarer word is spelled out as a first character plus -continuation pieces. So every word is representable and there is effectively no — the model can even invent plausible proper nouns letter by letter. Ask it questions Two interactions turn it from a thing you watch into a thing you experiment on: Knock parts out. Click any attention or MLP branch in the network, a single head's row in an attention panel, or a row of the attribution panel, and that component stops responding to the text. It still computes, so you still see its activations, but what it writes to the residual stream is replaced by its average output over real KJV text (mean-ablation; a knocked-out head has its slice replaced by its average before W_O ). The current step is recomputed at once on the same window with the same produced token, even while paused, and generation carries on with the broken model. A panel at the top of the right rail shows what the intact model would say on that exact window next to what the knocked-out one gives the same token and what it now says instead. Attribution says what wrote toward the token ; this is the experiment that says whether the model needed it. Knockouts are kept in the URL ( ?off=m0,a1h2 ), as is a custom prompt ( ?p=… ). Why the mean, not zero. Zeroing a part hands the later layers a value they never saw in training, so a big effect might be the model reacting to garbage rather than missing what the part knew. Mean-ablation removes only the information. The means live in ablation_means.json (11KB, from node tools/means.mjs : 600 seeded random 64-token windows of the corpus, 38,400 positions). It carries a fingerprint of the weights; a stale or missing file makes the page fall back to zero-ablation with a console warning. What you find. Measured on 40 windows from the held-out tail (2,520 next-word predictions), as the extra bits per token the knocked-out model needs to predict the real text (intact: 6.04 bits, top-1 right 25.8% of the time): knock out mean-ablation zero-ablation top-1 right (mean) : : : block 0 MLP +1.87 +1.86 10.0% block 0 attn +0.23 +0.26 22.3% blocks 1-3 MLP +0.14 to +0.16 +0.18 to +0.23 23.7-24.3% blocks 1-3 attn +0.06 to +0.10 +0.11 to +0.16 24.1-24.8% one head +0.02 or less (b0 head 0: +0.07) +0.06 or less 25% Block 0's MLP is the one that matters , and that survives the switch to mean-ablation unchanged, so it is not an artifact of zeros. Without it the model stutters: Thus saith the LORD; that I will will will put my my my Israel . Zero-ablation overstated everything else by roughly 20-100%: the later blocks refine the guess more gently than zeros suggested. Single heads barely matter (differences under 0.01 bits, including the small negative ones, are noise at this sample size): the four heads overlap enough that expect head knockouts to look like they do nothing. That is the result, not a bug. Inspect any word. Every word in the strip is tinted by how much it surprised the model ( -log2 p , red from 5 bits, full at 17). Hover or tap one to see the probability the model gave it, its rank, and the eight words it expected instead; click to pin the popover (this pauses generation), then pick an alternative to rewrite the text from that word on . title: Packing Explorer
desc: How efficiently can copies of a shape be packed into a container?
text: Packing explorer A browser-only packing experiment, mostly 2D: how tightly do N copies of a shape fit inside a container? The live view shows the current search; the smaller view always keeps the best feasible packing found so far. No replay or server-side solving is required. One container is curved. "Sphere (surface)" packs pieces onto a sphere's surface rather than into an outline: spherical caps for the circle the Tammes problem and regular spherical polygons for the rest. It has to be served over HTTP, since module workers cannot reliably run from file URLs. From the repo root: Open . The search starts as soon as the page loads and restarts whenever a control changes. Pause/Resume controls the worker; Reset restarts with a new random seed, as does Run again once a search has finished. The actual seed is shown below the attempt log and can be passed to PackingSolver to reproduce a run. The search uses several CPU cores: one module worker per core, less one left for the page, up to eight. Restarts are already independent no attempt hands the next anything but the global best so the workers never talk to each other; each runs the full restart budget from its own seed, and the page keeps the best layout any of them finds. Worker i runs seed seed + i , and only worker 0 opens from the aligned lattice ( latticeStart ), because that opening is the same whatever the seed. One worker at a time streams its live layout to the current-search view; the others report progress a few times a second, and the view hands over when the watched one finishes. As soon as any worker reaches the area lower bound, the rest are stopped. "s CPU" below the log sums compute time over all workers. The controls are mirrored into the query string ( ?container=&item=&n=&aspect= ), so a refresh keeps the current problem and a URL can be shared or bookmarked. Search and contact handling The outer loop shrinks the container, then attempts to repair overlaps at that fixed size. Failed repairs are inconclusive; they reduce the next shrink step and increase exploration. A feasible result updates the global best immediately. Efficiency is based exclusively on that saved feasible result. The aligned first start initially settles by translation only. This prevents unnecessary torque from disrupting a grid that can already tile its container. If sliding stalls, the solver retains the best result and retries the aligned start with rotation enabled. That work remains inside the same attempt budget. Scattered restarts use translation and rotation from the beginning. A result matching the area lower bound terminates the search early. Both the ordinary feasibility tolerance and the limits of floating-point arithmetic still apply. Plateaux are escaped by basin hopping : displace/rotate nearby groups at several scales, run bounded local settling, accept a reduction in normalized overlap energy (or a feasible layout), otherwise restore every coordinate and rotation. Independent restarts provide further exploration. This is an approximate local-search heuristic, not a guarantee of reaching an exact local or global minimum. An annealed-repair baseline (Metropolis acceptance over randomly perturbed pieces) was measured alongside it and removed: once a failed probe re-seeds (below), basin hopping was better on every case, because its group moves are what turn one arrangement into a differently-shaped one. A failed probe means the incumbent arrangement could not absorb the compression. Compressing it again only re-poses the same question, so by default the next probe scatters a fresh layout instead ( reseedAfterFailures ). The incumbent is still held, so an exploration that goes nowhere costs one probe and no ground. When the restarts are done, one last fine-grained shrink runs from the global best ( polishIterations ), which no restart would otherwise revisit. Those two matter most together. title: Particle Life
desc: 200,000 particles in eight colors, each attracted to or repelled by the others by a random rule. They gather into worms, cells, and swimmers. Runs on WebGPU.
text: Every pair of particles closer than core (a fraction of radius ) pushes apart, whatever their colors, and the push grows the closer they get (like 1/distance, capped). Past the core, out to the pair's reach, each pair of colors pulls together or pushes apart by its own random attraction (-1 to 1), strongest halfway out and fading to zero at both ends. The rules aren't symmetric, so red can chase blue while blue runs from red, and that's where the moving creatures come from. Reaches run from minReach to 1 times radius , so red might feel blue from far away but only notice other reds up close, which makes layered things like cells with insides. The core is what keeps blobs from collapsing. With a push that stays bounded, a blob of thousands of particles pulling inward always wins, and they pile into a single point; with one that grows as they get closer, packing them tighter always costs more than the pull can pay. repulsion and force are tuned together: weaker repulsion lets dense blobs come back, and too much of either (or very dense worlds, like a million particles with a small window) makes the steps overshoot and the whole world boil. If it boils, lower force or radius . The world wraps around at its edges, so nothing piles up against a wall and creatures can keep swimming. The attractions grid shows the rules: each row is a color, each column is the color it reacts to, green pulls and red pushes, and the size of the square is how far it reaches. Click a square to make it pull more, right-click or shift-click to make it push more, and scroll over it to change its reach. Hit new rules for a new random world. Changing the particle count scatters them again, changing the number of colors makes new rules, and the rest change the world live. The motion scales with radius , so a smaller radius with more particles gives the same behavior with more, smaller creatures. Scroll or pinch to zoom in where the pointer is, right-drag or shift-drag to pan, and double-click to see the whole world again. Dragging does whatever the tool is: stir drags particles along with the pointer. pull and push draw particles toward the pointer or blow them away. paint turns particles into the paint color. Click a color along the top of the grid to pick it. follow : click something and the camera stays on it. Each frame the GPU adds up where the particles near the middle of the screen are, and the camera drifts to their middle. pan drags the view. Particles are drawn as soft dots stretched back along their velocity ( streaks ), added into a float texture that fades by trails each frame, then tone mapped, so dense clusters glow toward white and moving ones leave tails. The URL hash holds the rules and any settings that differ from the defaults, so the address bar is always a link back to the current world (from a new random start). sim.js runs it on the GPU. Each step, particles are counted into grid cells one radius wide (atomic adds), a prefix sum turns the counts into where each cell starts, particles are copied into their cell's run, and then each one reads its 3x3 block of cells, adds up the forces, and moves. render.js draws the streaks, the trails, and the tone mapping. input.js handles the camera and the pointer tools. main.js has the settings, the rule grid, and the URL hash.

title: Primordial
desc: Matter that gathers into bodies, forages for food, carries its own rules, and evolves: 3D Flow-Lenia on WebGPU
text: A world of matter that only ever moves around, never appears or disappears. Every step, each of about ten kernels looks at the neighborhood of every cell (a few soft rings, out to some radius) and turns what it sees into "growth": a bump that's high when the neighborhood is just right. Matter then flows uphill on the summed growth, and away from crowding. That's the whole rule. Starting from an even haze, it gathers into bodies that wriggle, merge, split, stripe, and drift. There can be one, two, or three kinds of matter ( kinds of matter ). Each kernel looks at one kind and pushes another kind (or the same one) around, so one kind can wrap itself around another, push it along, or keep its distance. Crowding counts every kind, so they can't pile into the same place. The world is also covered in food. Dense matter eats it, matter is drawn toward where there's more ( hunger ), and it slowly grows back ( food regrows ). A body that drifts a little has fresh food ahead and eaten ground behind, so it keeps going: without food, many rules settle into bodies that sit still forever; with it, they keep swimming, turning, and changing shape. Too much hunger tears bodies apart, and how much is right depends on the rule. Eaten food shows as a faint blue glow, so bodies leave trails that fade as the food grows back. Shift-drag (or set drag to to stir) pushes matter along under the pointer, through the whole depth of the world. Matter also carries a genome: its own growth curve for each kernel (how strong it is, which neighborhood is just right, and how picky it is about that), its own hunger (how hard it's drawn to food, times hunger ), plus a lineage color. The rings each kernel looks through are shared by everyone, since they're what the FFTs use, but the growth curve is applied cell by cell afterward, so it costs nothing extra to let it differ. Each step, a cell takes on the genome from where its matter came from: it traces back along its flow, jittered by about as far as matter spreads, and copies the genome there. So the same matter can follow different rules in different places, and bodies carry their rules with them. With lineages above 1, the world starts split into regions, each with its own growth curves scattered around the rule's, colored by lineage: some gather into bodies, some stay a haze, and when bodies meet they mix cell by cell. Left alone, one lineage usually ends up owning nearly everything. mutations keeps it going: every so often a small ball of matter gets a new color and every kernel's growth curve nudged (stronger or weaker, centered higher or lower, pickier or more tolerant) and its hunger raised or lowered, and the new lineage either spreads or fades away. Since that changes what a good neighborhood is, a takeover can change the bodies' shape, not just their color: lumps can give way to one big body, then to a hollow tube. This is Flow-Lenia (Plantec et al. 2023), a mass-conserving version of Lenia, in 3D. Plain 3D Lenia mostly makes balls: its creatures live in narrow niches of rule space, and the stable ones are spheres. Because Flow-Lenia can't lose or make matter, nothing dies out or floods the world, and most random rules make something worth watching. sim.js runs it on the GPU. The neighborhoods are convolutions done with 3D FFTs ( fft.js ), two kernels per inverse FFT. Moving the matter uses reintegration tracking: each cell's matter lands as a small box wherever its flow sends it, and each cell sums the parts of its neighbors' boxes that overlap it, so nothing is lost. rule.js makes random rules (the ranges are from the paper; with several kinds of matter, each kind gets kernels pushing it from itself and from each other kind), nudges them, and packs them into the link. render.js raymarches the result: a lit surface where matter is dense, with soft shadows, ambient occlusion, and a glow from thinner matter. title: Stretchy Maps
desc: The world by country and the US by county, stretched so each area is proportional to a statistic
text: Stretchy Maps Contiguous cartograms of the world by country and the US by county: every region is resized so its area is proportional to a chosen metric, like median income or child mortality, while still touching the same neighbors. Alaska and Hawaii sit in insets off the lower left. Pick a map and a metric; the map stretches into shape as it's computed, and switching metrics glides from one shape to the next. Since area reads as an amount, the metric is multiplied by population by default (median income × population is roughly total income); untick "× population" to size by the rate itself. Color can show a second metric, so you can size countries by population and color them by income. How it works cartogram.js implements the flow-based cartogram of Gastner, Seguy & More (2018). The map's density (target area over current area, with the sea at the average) is rasterized onto a grid. Let the density slide linearly from that to perfectly even as t goes from 0 to 1. Mass is conserved if ρv = -∇Φ with ∇²Φ = ρ̄ - ρ0 , which doesn't depend on t, so one Poisson solve (by cosine transform) gives the whole flow, v = -∇Φ / ρ(t) . Every border point rides it from t = 0 to 1, so crowded regions spread out and sparse ones shrink. The flow itself never folds, but borders are straight segments between moving points, so where it's extreme (the Great Plains in US population) a few segments can cross. One run gets most of the way, and it repeats on its own output (with less initial blur each time) until under 0.5% of the area is in the wrong place. It runs in a worker. geometry.js turns TopoJSON into shared points, so neighboring regions share border points and stay stitched together. Long edges are split so they can bend, and the rings that cross the antimeridian (Chukotka, Fiji) are unwrapped. Positive values keep their exact ratios; a true zero gets a sliver, since a region can't vanish. Regions with no data keep their projected size relative to everything else (Albers USA draws Alaska at about a third of its true scale). Regions smaller than a grid cell, like Singapore or Manhattan, still get their full share, since their target is spread over the fine samples they cover. Shapes that share an ID, like Australia and its Ashmore and Cartier Islands, count as one region, and rings the simplified atlas collapsed to lines (Falls Church, VA) are dropped. Data data/ .json are built by node cartogram/buildData.js : Countries: Our World in Data grapher CSVs, latest year per country since 2000 US counties: County Health Rankings & Roadmaps 2025 Geometry comes from world-atlas and us-atlas on jsdelivr at runtime.

title: WebGPU Slime Mold
desc: A million agents following each other's scent trails, in three species that chase or avoid each other. Paint food and walls.
text: Runs on the GPU with WebGPU compute shaders, spawned in a disc in the middle. At startup it times a few steps and picks the grid resolution (up to full device resolution) and agent count (0.2 per cell, so about 1M on a laptop screen) to suit the GPU; the chosen size is logged to the console. Three species each lay their own trail channel and have their own color and behavior. follow1 – follow3 set how much a species follows (+) or avoids (-) each species' trail, including its own, so species can chase, flee, or ignore each other. Drag (or touch) the canvas to paint with the brush tool : food (gold) attracts every species and is slowly eaten ( appetite ); walls (gray) block agents, who also steer away from them. The eraser tool, right-drag, or shift-drag erases. reset restarts the colony but keeps the drawing, with eaten food restored, so you can draw a maze and replay it; clear drawing wipes it. Resizing the window also clears it. Performance: the trail is stored as f16 where supported, deposits are packed per-species counts in one u32 per cell, the blur goes through workgroup shared memory, and agents are periodically sorted by screen tile so their trail reads are cache-friendly. About 2.6 ms per step for 1M agents on a 3024×1656 grid (Apple Silicon). The number of steps per frame adapts to the GPU and the display's refresh rate ( pacer.js ), so the frame rate stays smooth and fast machines evolve quicker. Rendering draws the trails plus a faint dot per agent to an HDR texture, then tone maps and dithers it to the screen. Pick a look from the preset menu or hit randomize . The URL hash always holds the current settings (only the ones that differ from the defaults), so the address bar is always a shareable link. main.js – wiring and the frame loop simulation.js – buffers, agent/diffuse passes, reset sorter.js – periodically sorts agents by screen tile, for cache-friendly memory reads ( 4x faster) renderer.js – scene and tone-mapping render passes ( shaders/render.wgsl , shaders/post.wgsl ) pacer.js – adaptive steps per frame params.js – tunable parameters, defaults and ranges gui.js – the lil-gui controls presets.js – named presets and randomize share.js – syncs params with the URL hash uniforms.js – packs params into the uniform buffer (mirrors shaders/params.wgsl ) gpu.js – WebGPU setup and small helpers input.js – pointer tracking shaders/ – WGSL

title: Survival of the Fittest
desc: Each agent has a neural network which decides how to move using info about its surroundings. The ones that find food survive and reproduce.
text: Agents start with random weights. A brain never changes during an agent's life; the only way the population improves is that better foragers eat more, reach energy 1, and reproduce with mutation, while worse ones hit energy 0 and die. node benchmark.js scores a brain in isolation (fixed food field, no death or reproduction). The live sim can't tell you whether brains are improving, since food intake there is capped by the spawn rate rather than by skill. getPretrainedNetwork.js is not used by the sim. It supervises a net on "turn toward the food" and is kept only as a reference point for the benchmark - it's what a brain that genuinely uses its senses looks like. Note on measuring: benchmark.js scatters food uniformly, which rewards reactive sweeping only. In the live sim (where food grows in clumps) it gets the ranking backwards - brains with memory scored 106 there vs 140 without, yet sustained 27% more population in the sim. Sustained population is the honest measure; the benchmark is for catching gross decay.

title: Oscillating Reaction
desc: Spiral waves of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction. Drag to break a wave and watch its ends curl into spirals.
text: The Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction is a chemical mixture that keeps switching between two states instead of settling down. Spread thinly in a dish, it carries waves that look like these. Spirals and Target rings run the Oregonator, the standard model of the real chemistry, in its two-variable Tyson-Fife form. The colors follow the ferroin indicator a real dish uses: red-orange where the catalyst is reduced, blue where it's oxidized. Each wave's leading edge is drawn lighter. In a real dish, spirals form when a wave breaks. Drag across one to break it (the stroke resets the chemistry to rest), and its two free ends curl up into a pair of spirals turning opposite ways. Tap to set off a new wave. Target rings start at pacemakers, specks where the mixture oscillates on its own. In a real dish they're dust or bubbles. f sets how much bromide (the inhibitor) each reaction cycle makes. Above about 2.4 the mixture rests until a neighbor sets it off (an excitable medium). Below that it oscillates by itself, so the gaps between waves start flashing too. Nutshell is Alasdair Turner's 2009 "BZ reaction in a nutshell": three species eat each other rock-paper-scissors style, averaged over each 3×3 neighborhood every generation. It's a toy, not chemistry, but it makes a dense tangle of similar spirals. Everything runs on the GPU in WebGL2. The edges of the screen are walls, like the edge of a dish. The link records the preset, settings and random seed, so sharing it reproduces the starting pattern, but not anything drawn afterward.

title: People Network 3D
desc: A 3D network showing how similarly people answered a survey.
text: Everyone who took the survey rated themselves 1 to 10 on 36 traits. Each person is a dot, placed so that the distances between dots match the distances between their answers as well as 3D allows. Tap someone to see who they answered most and least like, and color everyone by any trait to see how it runs through the crowd. The layout is classical MDS refined by SMACOF stress majorization (embed.js). The page reports how far off the 3D distances are (Kruskal's stress-1, about 21% for raw answers), since 36 dimensions can't fit in 3 exactly. Lines are drawn from the real distances over all 36 answers, not from the 3D positions, so a long line is a pair the layout had to pull apart. "Compare by" uses the same two measures as People Stats: raw answer distance, or 1 minus the correlation of the answers. The URL keeps who is selected and the settings, so a link shows what you saw. If you picked yourself in People Stats, you get a yellow ring. Test the layout math with node peopleNetwork3D/embed.test.js .
